# Aristotle's Understanding of Motion, Time, and Temporal Awareness in the Soul

## Articulate Aristotle's Understanding of Motion and Time

The philosophical investigation of motion and time in Aristotelian thought reveals a fundamental interconnectedness that extends far beyond mere physical phenomena to encompass the very structure of human existence and temporal awareness. Aristotle's treatment of these concepts, particularly as they relate to the soul's capacity for perception and phantasia, demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of how beings encounter their world through temporally-structured experience. Indeed, the Greek conception of kinesis and chronos operates within what Heidegger identifies as a more primordial understanding of being as presence, or Anwesenheit, which grounds both motion and temporal awareness in the lived experience of being-in-the-world (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 7). This understanding challenges modern conceptions that treat motion and time as separate, objective phenomena; instead, Aristotle's analysis reveals them as co-constitutive aspects of the soul's dynamic engagement with its environment, where temporal awareness emerges through the soul's capacity to synthesize past, present, and future moments into coherent experience.

The significance of this Aristotelian framework becomes particularly evident when we consider how it anticipates contemporary insights into embodied cognition and temporal consciousness, suggesting that our understanding of time is not merely conceptual but fundamentally tied to the soul's kinetic engagement with the world. Thus, Aristotle's treatment of motion and time provides the foundation for understanding more complex phenomena such as phantasia and temporal unification, which depend upon the soul's basic capacity for temporal synthesis and its dynamic relationship to changing phenomena in the environment.

## Aristotle on Motion

Aristotle's conception of motion (kinesis) represents a radical departure from purely mechanistic understandings, positioning motion instead as a fundamental mode of being that characterizes living entities in their encounter with the world. Heidegger's interpretation illuminates this insight, noting that for Aristotle, "kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst"—motion is a way of being of Dasein itself, rather than merely a property that beings possess (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). This understanding emerges through Aristotle's complex analysis of the relationship between pathesis and poietikos, whose interanimation defines motion and "reaches into the true center of the Greek view of the world and life" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). Motion, accordingly, cannot be understood as simply the displacement of objects in space, but rather as the actualization of potentiality within beings that are fundamentally characterized by their capacity for change and development.

The sophistication of Aristotle's analysis becomes apparent in his definition of motion as "the fulfilment of the alterable as alterable," which Heidegger translates as "Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). This formulation reveals motion as inherently relational, involving both active and passive dimensions that cannot be separated without distorting the phenomenon itself. The emphasis on "ein anderes Bewegendes"—another mover—suggests that motion is not simply the action of one entity upon another, but rather a complex interplay in which the moved is itself always already a mover, participating actively in its own transformation.

This conception of motion proves particularly crucial for understanding how living beings encounter their environment, since (White 1985) perception, cognition, and action are all fundamentally kinetic processes involving the dynamic interaction between the soul and its world. Hence, motion serves as the ontological ground for more complex phenomena such as temporal awareness and phantasia, both of which depend upon the soul's capacity for dynamic engagement with changing phenomena over time.

## Aristotle on Time

Aristotle's understanding of time emerges from his analysis of motion, yet it reveals temporal awareness as a distinct phenomenon that requires the soul's synthetic activity to constitute coherent temporal experience. John Bowin's  for Aristotle, "the discriminating power and the time of its exercise must be one and undivided" (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 17), indicating that temporal awareness involves a unified faculty that can simultaneously grasp different temporal moments. This synthetic capacity proves essential for understanding how the soul constitutes temporal experience, since without it, temporal awareness would collapse into a series of disconnected moments rather than the unified flow of experience that characterizes conscious life.

The complexity of Aristotle's temporal analysis becomes evident when we consider how time relates to both motion and the soul's capacity for measurement and comparison. Time is not simply the measure of motion, as is often suggested, but rather emerges through the soul's active engagement with changing phenomena, whereby temporal relationships become manifest through the soul's capacity to hold together past, present, and future moments in unified experience. This process involves what might be called temporal synthesis, wherein the soul actively constitutes temporal relationships rather than passively receiving temporal impressions from the environment.

Furthermore, Aristotle's  temporal awareness is fundamentally tied to the soul's capacity for phantasia, since temporal relationships often involve the soul's ability to imagine or re-present experiences that are not immediately present to sensation. The future, in particular, can only be grasped through the soul's capacity to project beyond immediate experience, while the past requires the soul's ability to retain and re-present previous experiences in modified form. Thus, temporal awareness emerges as a complex achievement of the soul's synthetic activity rather than a simple given of conscious experience.

## The Relation Between Motion and Time

The relationship between motion and time in Aristotelian thought reveals a fundamental interdependence that challenges any attempt to treat these phenomena as separate or independent. Motion provides the ontological ground for temporal experience, while time emerges through the soul's synthetic activity in relation to changing phenomena; yet neither can be adequately understood without reference to the other, since motion without temporal structure would be incoherent, while time without kinetic content would be empty. This  both motion and time are fundamentally relational phenomena that emerge through the dynamic interaction between the soul and its environment, rather than objective features of the world that exist independently of conscious experience.

Heidegger's interpretation illuminates this relationship by showing how both motion and time are grounded in what he calls the "kinetic ambiguity of Being-in-the-world," wherein the soul's engagement with its environment involves both active and passive dimensions that cannot be clearly separated (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). The soul is simultaneously moved by its environment and actively moving within that environment, participating in a complex dance of reciprocal influence that constitutes both motion and temporal experience. This kinetic ambiguity proves essential for understanding how temporal awareness emerges, since (White 1985) the soul's relationship to time is not simply one of passive reception but of active participation in the constitution of temporal relationships.

Moreover, the relationship between motion and time proves crucial for understanding how the soul's various capacities—perception, phantasia, desire, and action—work together to constitute coherent experience. Each of these capacities involves both kinetic and temporal dimensions, since they all require the soul's ability to engage dynamically with changing phenomena over time. Perception involves the soul's kinetic response to environmental changes, phantasia requires the temporal synthesis of past and present experience, desire projects toward future possibilities, and action involves the temporal coordination of intention and execution. Hence, the relationship between motion and time provides the fundamental structure within which all of the soul's activities unfold.

## Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Aristotelian aisthesis (perception) reveals temporal awareness as emerging through the soul's discriminating activity rather than through passive reception of temporal impressions, demonstrating how perceptual awareness is fundamentally structured by temporal synthesis and kinetic engagement with the environment. The soul's capacity for temporal discrimination involves what Bowin identifies as a unified discriminating power that can simultaneously grasp different temporal moments, suggesting that temporal awareness emerges through the soul's active comparison and synthesis of perceptual content over time (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 17). This process involves more than simple succession, since it requires the soul's ability to hold together past and present perceptions in unified experience, thereby constituting temporal relationships through its own synthetic activity.

The sophistication of this analysis becomes apparent when we consider how perception involves both immediate responsiveness to environmental changes and the capacity for temporal comparison that enables the soul to distinguish between different types of change. Without this temporal dimension, perception would collapse into a series of disconnected moments rather than the continuous flow of experience that characterizes conscious life. The soul's capacity for temporal synthesis thus proves essential for perceptual awareness, since it enables the soul to constitute coherent perceptual objects that persist through time and change.

Furthermore, the relationship between aisthesis and temporal awareness reveals how perception is fundamentally kinetic, involving the soul's dynamic engagement with changing phenomena rather than passive reception of static impressions. This kinetic dimension proves crucial for understanding how temporal awareness emerges, since (White 1985) the soul's relationship to time is not simply one of measurement but of active participation in temporal processes. The soul does not simply observe temporal change but participates in it, constituting temporal relationships through its own perceptual activity.

## Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Aristotelian phantasia emerges as the crucial faculty that enables temporal unification by synthesizing past perceptual experience with present awareness and future projection, revealing how the soul constitutes coherent temporal experience beyond the immediate deliverances of sensation. Ned O'Gorman's  phantasia operates as "comparative seeing" that enables the soul to grasp relationships and magnitudes that exceed immediate perceptual content (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 12). This comparative dimension proves essential for temporal unification, since it enables the soul to synthesize experiences from different temporal moments into unified awareness, thereby constituting the temporal structure that characterizes conscious life.

The temporal function of phantasia becomes particularly evident in phenomena such as fear, where, as Heidegger notes, the soul responds not to immediate perceptual content but to "phantasmata of some destructive or painful evil in the future" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 10). This capacity to respond to imagined future possibilities demonstrates phantasia's essential role in temporal synthesis, since it enables the soul to project beyond immediate experience and constitute temporal relationships that span past, present, and future. Fear thus reveals phantasia as operating in what Heidegger identifies as the "peculiar tense, voice, and mode" of the possible future, characterized by "ein Nicht-Dasein im Sichnahern zu sein"—a not-being in the process of approaching (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 10).

Moreover, phantasia's role in temporal unification proves crucial for understanding how the soul constitutes meaningful experience, since meaning often depends upon the ability to synthesize experiences from different temporal contexts into coherent patterns. The soul's capacity for phantasia thus enables it to constitute temporal relationships that exceed immediate experience, providing the foundation for more complex phenomena such as memory, anticipation, deliberation, and practical wisdom, all of which require the ability to synthesize past experience with present awareness and future projection.

## Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian motion, time, and temporal awareness reveals these phenomena as fundamentally existential structures that constitute the basic character of human being-in-the-world, rather than merely objective features of the natural world that can be studied from a detached theoretical perspective. His  kinesis provides "the authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being," indicating that motion and temporality are not accidents of human existence but rather constitute the fundamental structure within which human being unfolds (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 10). This interpretation challenges traditional approaches that treat motion and time as separate from human existence, revealing instead how they are intimately woven into the fabric of human being-in-the-world.

The significance of Heidegger's interpretation becomes apparent in his analysis of the pathe (passions), which he reads not as mere psychological states but as "Befindlichkeiten, dispositions" that reveal fundamental structures of temporal existence (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 10). These dispositions are fundamentally temporal, oriented toward past, present, and future in ways that constitute the basic temporal structure of human existence. Hence, Heidegger's interpretation reveals how Aristotelian psychology anticipates existential analytics, showing how phenomena such as fear, desire, and deliberation reveal fundamental temporal structures rather than merely contingent psychological states.

Furthermore, Heidegger's interpretation illuminates how Aristotelian kinesis anticipates insights into the temporal structure of existence by revealing motion as a fundamental "way of being" rather than merely a physical property. This understanding proves crucial for comprehending how temporal awareness emerges, since (White 1985) the soul's relationship to time is not simply cognitive but ontological, involving the fundamental structure of existence itself. Thus, Heidegger's interpretation reveals Aristotelian motion and time as anticipating existential insights into the temporal structure of human being-in-the-world, providing resources for understanding how temporal awareness emerges through the soul's fundamental engagement with its environment rather than through detached theoretical observation.

Indeed, the convergence between Aristotelian and Heideggerian  temporal awareness cannot be adequately understood without reference to the existential structures that constitute human being-in-the-world, indicating that any complete account of motion, time, and temporal consciousness must attend to the fundamental ways in which human existence is temporally structured from the outset.
